Introducing Gaussian Process regression models¶

This post introduces Gaussian Process (GP) regression models and sets the stage for later posts that apply them to real-world data, with examples from spatial analytics and insurance pricing. The key formulas are presented and implemented in Python to build intuition for how they work.

Why Gaussian Processes?¶

GPs are non-parametric, meaning that rather than assuming a fixed functional form for $f(x)$, they place a prior directly over functions. This allows them flexibly fit non-linear relationships and provide uncertainty estimates for each prediction. This isn't to say there are no parameters. The kernel has hyperparameters (e.g. a length scale and variance) that are learned from data. The prior is not assumption-free either, as the choice of kernel encodes assumptions such as smoothness. But the model's complexity is not limited by a fixed number of parameters and will grow as the dataset does.

For regression, we assume the observed data is the function plus Gaussian noise, and that function values at any finite set of inputs are jointly Gaussian. This post covers that Gaussian-likelihood case.

Multivariate Gaussian refresher¶

For a $d$-dimensional vector $\boldsymbol{y} = f(x)$ with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$:

$$p(\boldsymbol{f(x)} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = (2\pi)^{-d/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{-1/2} \exp\left\{ -\tfrac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{f(x)}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{f(x)}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \right\}$$

Multivariate Gaussians are closed under marginalisation and conditioning, which is what makes GP prediction tractable. Suppose $\boldsymbol{f(x)} = (\boldsymbol{y}_1, \boldsymbol{y}_2)$ is jointly Gaussian with

$$ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} \end{pmatrix}. $$

The marginals are obtained by selecting the corresponding entries of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and blocks of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, so any subset of a multivariate Gaussian is also Gaussian:

$$ \begin{aligned} p(\boldsymbol{y}_1) &= \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}_1 \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_1, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}) \\ p(\boldsymbol{y}_2) &= \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}_2 \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_2, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}) \end{aligned} $$

The conditional is also Gaussian. Its mean is an affine function of $\boldsymbol{y}_2$, and its covariance does not depend on the observed value of $\boldsymbol{y}_2$:

$$ \begin{aligned} p(\boldsymbol{y}_1 \mid \boldsymbol{y}_2) &= \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}_1 \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2}) \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2} &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1} (\boldsymbol{y}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2) \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2} &= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} \end{aligned} $$

In GP regression, $\boldsymbol{y}_2$ will be the observed training values and $\boldsymbol{y}_1$ the function values at new inputs, so this conditional is the posterior predictive distribution.

For the full derivation, see Murphy, 2022, Section 3.2.3.

What is a Gaussian Process?¶

A Gaussian process (GP) is defined as a distribution over functions $f: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ with the property that, for any finite set of inputs $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the vector $\mathbf{f} = [f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)]^\top$ has a joint multivariate Gaussian distribution (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006, Murphy, 2022). A GP can be specified by a mean function $m(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x)]$ and a positive semi-definite covariance function (kernel) $k(x, x') = \mathrm{Cov}(f(x), f(x'))$:

$$f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m(x), k(x, x')),$$

so that $\mathbf{f} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{K})$ with $m_i = m(x_i)$ and $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$.

Given $\mathcal{X}$ could take infinitely many input values, a GP can also be viewed as an infinite-dimensional generalisation of the multivariate Gaussian, with one random variable $f(x)$ per input location. In practice, we only evaluate the function for as many points we have data for, collapsing the infinite-dimensional GP into a finite-dimensional multivariate Gaussian distribution, with $\text{n dimensions}$ as equal to $\text{n data points}$. The collapse process is achieved by marginalising over the infinitely unobserved dimensions.

The kernel¶

The kernel (covariance function) specifies how the values of $f$ at different inputs relate to each other, i.e. it measures their similarity. Given inputs $x_1, \dots, x_n$, it produces the covariance matrix $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$. Taking a zero mean function for simplicity, the GP prior at those inputs is

$$\mathbf{f} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, K).$$

A large value of $k(x, x')$ means $f(x)$ and $f(x')$ are strongly correlated, so observing $f$ at one input is informative about $f$ at the other. A valid kernel must give a symmetric positive semi-definite $K$ for any set of inputs. Common choices include the squared exponential and the Matérn family, which are stationary, meaning they depend only on the distance between inputs, and the covariance decays as that distance grows. The kernel also encodes assumptions about smoothness.

The squared exponential kernel is

$$ k_{\mathrm{SE}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\left(-\frac{\|x-x'\|^2}{2\ell^2}\right). $$

The lengthscale $\ell$ controls how quickly the correlation decays with distance (small $\ell$ gives wiggly functions, large $\ell$ smooth ones), and the signal variance $\sigma_f^2$ is the prior variance of $f(x)$, controlling how far the function typically deviates from its mean. These are hyperparameters learned from the data, either by maximising the marginal likelihood or by placing priors on them in a Bayesian treatment.

Plotting the Kernel¶

To better understand the squared exponential function (or Radial Basis Function), we can plot how the covariance ($k$) values change as we change the distance $\ell$ parameter. If we decrease $\ell$ to the minimum, notice how even a small step from the mean will sharply reduce our expected covariance (left plot) and the covariance $K$ approaches the diagonol (right plot), i.e. points are independent. As we increase the distance, the scale that we consider $X$ values as similar increases and the curve decays more slowly (left plot) and the diagonol $K$ widens, meaning more distant points are related.

Show code
In [1]:
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

def kernel(X1, X2, ell=1.0, sigma2=1.0):
    r = cdist(X1, X2) / ell

    return sigma2 * np.exp(-0.5 * r**2)


x_coarse = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)[:, None]
d_grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)

GP regression¶

Earlier we derived the conditional distribution for a Gaussian split into two blocks. For GP regression, the blocks are the observed training outputs $\mathbf{y}$ and the unseen function values $\mathbf{f}_*$ at test inputs $X_*$. We allow for noisy observations $y_i = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i$, with $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)$, so the joint distribution is

$$ \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{y} \\ \mathbf{f}_* \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}_X \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_* \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} K_\sigma & K_{X,*} \\ K_{*,X} & K_{*,*} \end{pmatrix}\right), \qquad K_\sigma = K_{X,X} + \sigma_n^2 I_N, $$

where $K_{*,X} = K_{X,*}^\top$. The posterior predictive density at test points $X_*$ is then

$$ p(\mathbf{f}_* \mid X_*, X, \mathbf{y}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{f}_* \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{*|X}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{*|X}), $$

$$ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{*|X} &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_* + K_{*,X} K_\sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_X), \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{*|X} &= K_{*,*} - K_{*,X} K_\sigma^{-1} K_{X,*}. \end{aligned} $$

With a zero mean function ($\boldsymbol{\mu}_X = \boldsymbol{\mu}_* = \mathbf{0}$) and $A = K_\sigma^{-1} K_{X,*}$, these simplify to

$$ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{*|X} &= K_{*,X} (K_\sigma^{-1} \mathbf{y}) = A^\top \mathbf{y}, \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{*|X} &= K_{*,*} - A^\top K_{X,*}. \end{aligned} $$

The conditional mean can be thought of as a weighted average of $\mathbf{y}$, with the kernel up-weighting nearby observations. The covariance is our prior uncertainty $K_{**}$, minus that which is explained by the data. The noise term $\sigma_n^2$ dictates how much we trust the observed data relative to the prior.

The posterior distribution above can codified as follows:

Show code
In [4]:
def gp_posterior(X, y, Xs, ell, sigma2, noise):
    """Posterior mean and covariance of f at Xs, given noisy observations y at X."""
    Kxx = kernel(X, X, ell=ell, sigma2=sigma2) + noise * np.eye(len(X))  # K + σn² I
    Kxs = kernel(X, Xs, ell=ell, sigma2=sigma2)
    Kss = kernel(Xs, Xs, ell=ell, sigma2=sigma2)
    A = np.linalg.solve(Kxx, Kxs)
    mu = A.T @ y
    sig = Kss - A.T @ Kxs
    return mu, sig

1-D simulated data¶

We can first define our observed $X$ as drawn from a uniform distribution $[0,10]$ and $y$ a linear function of the true underlying function $f$ plus some noise $\epsilon$.

Show code
In [5]:
SIGMA2, NOISE, SEED = 1.0, 0.1, 1   # fixed; only ℓ or n is swept

def f_true_1d(X):
    return np.sin(1.2 * X[:, 0]) + 0.5 * np.cos(2.5 * X[:, 0])

def make_data(seed, n, dim, f_true):
    """n noisy observations at random locations in [0, 10]^dim; the first k points are the same for any n >= k."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.uniform(0, 10, (n, dim))
    e = rng.standard_normal(n)
    y = f_true(X) + 0.3 * e 
    return X, y

n_example, ell_example = 200, 2

X, y = make_data(SEED, n_example, 1, f_true_1d)
print(X.shape, y.shape)

(200, 1) (200,)

The unseen function values $\mathbf{f}_*$ are to be evaluated across an evenly spaced grid of test inputs $X_*$.

Show code
In [6]:
x_grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 150)[:, None]  # 1-D locations used throughout
xs = x_grid[:, 0]

mu, S = gp_posterior(X, y, x_grid, ell_example, SIGMA2, NOISE)
print(mu.shape, S.shape)

(150,) (150, 150)
Show code
In [7]:
N_POST = 5  # posterior sample curves available
LINE_TRACES = [0, 1, 2, 3, *range(5, 5 + N_POST)]  # every trace except the observation markers (4)
MAX_SAMPLES = 10

def plotly_slider(values, label, start):
    """A Plotly slider that steps through frames named str(value)."""
    return dict(active=values.index(start), pad=dict(t=50), currentvalue=dict(prefix=f"{label} = "),
                steps=[dict(method="animate", label=f"{v:g}",
                            args=[[str(v)], dict(mode="immediate",
                                                 frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True),
                                                 transition=dict(duration=0))])
                       for v in values])
def sample_gp(K, n_samples, rng):
    """Draw n_samples functions from N(0, K); returns shape (n, n_samples)."""
    return rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(len(K)), K, size=n_samples).T

def curves(ell, n, n_post=N_POST):
    """All traces for one slider position."""
    X, y = make_data(SEED, n, 1, f_true_1d)
    mu, S = gp_posterior(X, y, x_grid, ell, SIGMA2, NOISE)
    sd = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.diag(S), 0, None))
    F = mu[:, None] + sample_gp(S, n_post, np.random.default_rng(SEED))   # was N_POST

    x, r = np.round(xs, 3), lambda a: np.round(a, 3)
    return [
        go.Scatter(x=x, y=r(mu + 2 * sd), mode="lines", line=dict(width=0), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"),
        go.Scatter(x=x, y=r(mu - 2 * sd), mode="lines", line=dict(width=0), fill="tonexty",
                   fillcolor="rgba(31,119,180,0.2)", name="posterior mean ± 2 sd"),
        go.Scatter(x=x, y=r(mu), mode="lines", line=dict(color=COLORS["mean"], width=3), name="posterior mean"),
        go.Scatter(x=x, y=r(f_true_1d(x_grid)), mode="lines",
                   line=dict(color=COLORS["truth"], dash="dash"), name="true f"),
        go.Scatter(x=r(X[:, 0]), y=r(y), mode="markers",
                   marker=dict(color=COLORS["data"], size=8), name="observations y"),
        *[go.Scatter(x=x, y=r(F[:, i]), mode="lines", line=dict(width=1), opacity=0.6,
                     name="posterior samples", legendgroup="samples", showlegend=(i == 0))
          for i in range(n_post)],
    ]

def posterior_fig(make, values, label, start):
    fig = go.Figure(data=make(start), frames=[go.Frame(name=str(v), data=make(v)) for v in values])
    fig.update_traces(visible="legendonly", selector=dict(legendgroup="samples"))  # hidden until legend click
    fig.update_layout(height=520, xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="f(x)", yaxis_range=[-5, 5],
                      margin=dict(t=60, b=90), legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.1),
                      sliders=[plotly_slider(values, label, start)])
    return fig

def draws_fig(ell=1.0, n=8, max_draws=20):
    base = 5  # traces before the samples: band top, band bottom, mean, true f, observations
    fig = go.Figure(curves(ell, n, n_post=max_draws))
    fig.update_traces(visible=False, selector=dict(legendgroup="samples"))   # start with no draws shown
    fig.update_layout(
        height=520, xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="f(x)", yaxis_range=[-5, 5],
        margin=dict(t=60, b=90), legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.1),
        sliders=[dict(
            active=0, pad=dict(t=50), currentvalue=dict(prefix="posterior draws = "),
            steps=[dict(method="restyle", label=str(k),
                        args=[dict(visible=[True] * base + [i < k for i in range(max_draws)])])
                   for k in range(max_draws + 1)])])
    return fig
Adjusting the lengthscale hyperparameter $\ell$¶

To see how the posterior predictive mean changes as we adjust the lengthscale, we can adjust the slider for a range of possible $\ell$ values. Adjusting the lengthscale $\ell$ smaller introduces more oscilation in $f(x)$ away from $0$, while increasing moves neighbouring lines together more smoothly around the mean.

Show code
In [8]:
ells = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0]
ns = list(range(1, 31))
Show code
In [9]:
fig_ell = posterior_fig(lambda ell: curves(ell, 8), ells, "lengthscale ℓ", start=1.0)
fig_ell
Sampling from the GP prior¶

Before we see any data, we assume that $\mathbf f\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,K)$, which is to say that it is a random variable with entries correlated according to $K$. Random samples from $f$ are realisations of the Gaussian Process at finite points. The below sample_gp function draws such random samples according to a multivariate normal distribution using the $K$ built from our simulated input data.

Show code
In [10]:
def sample_gp(K, n_samples, rng):
    """Draw n_samples functions from N(0, K); returns shape (n, n_samples)."""
    return rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(len(K)), K, size=n_samples).T
Show code
In [11]:
fig_n   = posterior_fig(lambda n: curves(1.0, n), ns, "observations n", start=8)
fig_draws = draws_fig()
fig_draws.show()
Reducing undertainty with scale¶

As the number of observations $n$ increases, the model's effective degrees of freedom grow and posterior uncertainty shrinks near observed inputs $X$, tightening the fit to the underlying function $f$.

Show code
In [12]:
fig_n

2-D simulated data¶

GPs also extends from 1-D curves to spatial fields (and higher dimensional inputs) dimenions, making them useful for approximating unknown spatial functions.

First, we again simulate observed $X$ and $y$ data as our inputs for the GP to learn from. The true function $f$ should create several alternating peaks and troughs across the domain.

Show code
In [13]:
def f_true_2d(X):
    return np.sin(0.8 * X[:, 0]) * np.cos(0.6 * X[:, 1])   # my choice of true surface

# one fixed pool of noisy observations; the n slider uses the first n, so points are only ever added
X_all, y_all = make_data(SEED, 100, 2, f_true_2d)

And define a 2-d grid of test points $X_{*1}, X_{*2}$, with the posterior evaluated over a 20x20 grid of 400 test points.

Show code
In [14]:
g = np.linspace(0, 10, 20)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(g, g)
X2 = np.column_stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()])  # 400 grid locations (x, y); reshape(20, 20) gives rows = y

truth = f_true_2d(X2).reshape(20, 20)
Show code
In [15]:
def fit(ell, n):
    X, y = X_all[:n], y_all[:n]
    mu, _ = gp_posterior(X, y, X2, ell, SIGMA2, NOISE)
    est = mu.reshape(20, 20)
    return [go.Heatmap(z=np.round(est, 3)),
            go.Heatmap(z=np.round(np.abs(est - truth), 3)),
            go.Scatter(x=np.round(X[:, 0], 2), y=np.round(X[:, 1], 2))]

def fit_fig(make, values, label, start):
    est0, err0, obs0 = make(start)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, horizontal_spacing=0.12,
                        subplot_titles=("True f", "GP estimate (posterior mean)", "Absolute error"))
    fig.add_heatmap(x=g, y=g, z=np.round(truth, 3), coloraxis="coloraxis", row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_heatmap(x=g, y=g, z=est0.z, coloraxis="coloraxis", row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_heatmap(x=g, y=g, z=err0.z, coloraxis="coloraxis2", row=1, col=3)
    fig.add_scatter(x=obs0.x, y=obs0.y, mode="markers", showlegend=False, row=1, col=2,
                    marker=dict(color="white", size=6, line=dict(color="black", width=1)))
    fig.frames = [go.Frame(name=str(v), traces=[1, 2, 3], data=make(v)) for v in values]
    fig.update_layout(
        height=420, margin=dict(t=50, b=110),
        coloraxis=dict(colorscale="RdBu_r", cmin=-1.2, cmax=1.2,
                       colorbar=dict(title=dict(text="f"), x=0.64, len=0.85, thickness=12)),
        coloraxis2=dict(colorscale="Viridis", cmin=0, cmax=1,
                        colorbar=dict(title=dict(text="|error|"), x=1.02, len=0.85, thickness=12)),
        sliders=[plotly_slider(values, label, start)])
    return fig

Scaling $\ell$¶

With an $\ell$ is very small, the kernel placed over each point has a rapid correlation decay with distance and each observation influences onlys its immediate neighbourhood. This produces localised bumps around each point. Increasing $\ell$ allows information from each point to propogate across further distances, better capturing smooth underlying surface of $f_{\text{true}}$. However, taking $\ell$ too far eventually over-smooths the alternating peaks and troughs of $f_{\text{true}}$.

Show code
In [16]:
ells2 = [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0]
Show code
In [17]:
fit_ell = fit_fig(lambda ell: fit(ell, 40), ells2, "lengthscale ℓ", start=1.5)

fit_ell
Increasing $n$¶

As $n$ is increased, the GP estimate of $f_{\text{true}}$ better approximates the true surface, reflected in the decreasing absolute error shown on the right.

Show code
In [18]:
ns2 = [2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, 100]
Show code
In [19]:
fit_n   = fit_fig(lambda n: fit(1.5, n), ns2, "observations n", start=40)
fit_n

Next steps¶

This post introduced Gaussian processes under the assumption of a Gaussian likelihood, which allows us to compute the posterior distribution analytically. In practice, however, data often follows non-Gaussian distributions, such as binary outcomes (Bernoulli) or counts (Poisson), where exact inference is intractable. In the next post, we will explore how to extend Gaussian processes to non-Gaussian likelihoods using approximation methods.
